questions.prompt: Which statement best describes how the terms AI, machine learning and large language models relate to each other?

options.text: They are three names for the same technology.
options.explanation: They are related but not the same. Each is a narrower part of the one before it.

options.text: AI is the broad umbrella, machine learning is one approach within it, and LLMs are a specialised kind of (deep) machine learning.
options.explanation: Right. Think of nested circles: AI contains machine learning, which contains deep learning, which contains LLMs.

options.text: LLMs are the broadest category, and AI is one type of LLM.
options.explanation: This is backwards. LLMs are the most specialised of the three.

options.text: Machine learning is the old version of AI and has been replaced by LLMs.
options.explanation: Machine learning is still everywhere (spam filters, bank fraud checks). LLMs are a type of machine learning, not a replacement for it.

questions.prompt: A plumber wants customers to get an automatic text the day before every booked appointment. What does this need?

options.text: A large language model
options.explanation: There is nothing to write or interpret. The message is fixed, so an LLM adds cost and unpredictability for no benefit.

options.text: A custom-trained machine-learning model
options.explanation: There's no pattern to learn. The rule is simple and known in advance.

options.text: Plain rules-based automation, often a feature of the booking software
options.explanation: Correct. 'One day before the appointment, send this text' is a fixed rule. No AI is needed, and saying so builds trust.

options.text: Deep learning
options.explanation: Deep learning is for complex pattern recognition such as images or speech, not for scheduled reminders.

questions.prompt: Which of these are true of large language models such as the ones inside ChatGPT, Claude and Gemini? Choose all that apply.

options.text: They are trained to predict the next word across huge amounts of text.
options.explanation: Yes. Next-word prediction at enormous scale is the core training task.

options.text: They look up facts in a database, so their answers are always accurate.
options.explanation: No. They generate statistically likely text, which can be confidently wrong. This is called hallucination.

options.text: They automatically learn a client's prices and procedures once the client starts using them.
options.explanation: No. By default they only know their training data and what you put in the conversation. Giving them business knowledge is a design task.

options.text: They are a type of generative AI.
options.explanation: Yes. They create new content (text) rather than only sorting or scoring existing content.

questions.scenario: A roofing firm sends about 250 quotes a year. The owner asks you to 'build an AI that predicts which quotes we'll win'.
questions.prompt: What is the most honest and useful advice?

options.text: Build a custom machine-learning model straight away: AI can predict anything.
options.explanation: With so few examples a model would be unreliable, and the client would pay for something that doesn't work.

options.text: Explain that this is a machine-learning problem but there isn't enough data yet; start recording won and lost reasons consistently, and revisit later.
options.explanation: Correct. You identify the right technology, explain the data limit honestly, and set up the groundwork, all of which builds trust.

options.text: Tell them AI cannot help with sales at all.
options.explanation: Too dismissive. AI can help with follow-ups, quote writing and more. This particular prediction task just isn't ready yet.

options.text: Ask ChatGPT to guess which quotes they'll win.
options.explanation: An LLM given no outcome data would just produce plausible-sounding guesses. That is exactly the kind of misuse to avoid.

questions.prompt: A client says: 'We tried ChatGPT last year and it was rubbish.' Why is it useful to know the difference between a product and a model?

options.text: Because ChatGPT is not an AI product.
options.explanation: ChatGPT is an AI product. It is OpenAI's app, built on their GPT models.

options.text: Because the model inside a product changes over time, and free tiers may use different models than paid ones, so their experience may not reflect what is possible now.
options.explanation: Correct. Products swap and upgrade models regularly, so an old or free-tier experience is a weak guide to current capability, and to how a well-designed workflow would perform.

options.text: Because models never change, so the client must have used it wrongly.
options.explanation: Models change often. Blaming the client is also a poor sales move.

options.text: It isn't useful: all AI products use the same model.
options.explanation: Different companies build different models (GPT, Claude, Gemini), and each company has several of them.
